prompt:
Research what the Rust project officially documents about its release cadence and how long each stable version is supported. Cite the official Rust page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Based on the official Rust documentation, here is the information about Rust's release cadence and support policy.

Rust follows a predictable six-week release cycle for new stable versions. This is described in the Rust Book appendix on Nightly Rust, which explains the "train model" release process.

**Release Cadence:**
[doc.rust-lang.org](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html) | QUOTE: "Rust releases every six weeks, like clockwork." | CLAIM: Rust has a regular six-week release cycle

**Support Policy:**
The same source explicitly states that each stable version is supported for six weeks, after which it reaches end of life when the next version is released.

[doc.rust-lang.org](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/appendix-07-nightly-rust.html) | QUOTE: "The Rust project supports the most recent stable version. When a new stable version is released, the old version reaches its end of life (EOL). This means each version is supported for six weeks." | CLAIM: Each stable Rust version is supported for exactly six weeks

This six-week support window is consistent with the six-week release cycle, meaning only the latest stable version receives official support from the Rust project at any given time.
